articles.title: VÍDEO: Policial atira em pit bulls que atacavam pessoas em MG | G1
articles.standfirst: Câmera corporal registrou o momento em que policial disparou contra dois animais, que atacavam um idoso de 65 anos, em São Gonçalo do Pará. Segundo a PM, os cães voltaram a apresentar comportamento agressivo e foram mortos após novas ocorrências.
articles.summary: Câmera corporal registrou o momento em que policial disparou contra os animais, que atacavam um idoso de 65 anos, em São Gonçalo do Pará.
articles.body:
Um policial militar atirou contra dois cães da raça pit bull que estavam soltos na rua e atacando pessoas em São Gonçalo do Pará , no Centro-Oeste de Minas, neste domingo (1º). A ação foi registrada pela câmera corporal do policial (veja acima) . Após novas denúncias, os animais foram mortos pela corporação.

As imagens mostram a viatura parando na rua. Em seguida, o militar desce do veículo e atira diversas vezes contra os cães, que saem correndo. Os animais estavam atacando um idoso de 65 anos, que já estava caído no chão.

De acordo com o boletim de ocorrência, os militares foram acionados inicialmente por um morador, que denunciou que os dois cães estavam atacando outro animal em uma rua da cidade.

Durante o deslocamento até o endereço, os policiais encontraram o idoso caído no chão e sendo atacado pelos animais.

O militar efetuou disparos para interromper o ataque. A vítima foi socorrida e encaminhada ao hospital.

No local, os policiais também encontraram outra pessoa que havia sido atacada pelos mesmos cães.

Policial atirou em cães que estavam atacando idoso — Foto: PM/Divulgação

Mesmo após a primeira intervenção, moradores continuaram acionando a polícia e relatando que os animais continuavam circulando pela cidade e apresentavam comportamento agressivo.

Diante das novas ocorrências, os militares localizaram os cães novamente e decidiram abatê-los. Conforme o registro policial, a decisão considerou o histórico de ataques, o comportamento dos animais e o risco à integridade física de outras pessoas.

Após a morte dos animais, a tutora, de 29 anos, compareceu ao local. Segundo o relato dela à polícia, os cães fugiram do canil mantido na residência após um descuido dos enteados, que também moram no imóvel.

A mulher já havia sido presa no ano passado em razão de um ataque envolvendo os mesmos animais. Na ocasião, os cães atacaram uma idosa de 85 anos, que sofreu ferimentos graves.

Segundo a Polícia Militar, a reincidência dos ataques e a gravidade dos episódios foram consideradas na decisão de abater os animais.

articles.body: The Department of Artificial Intelligence and Data Science (AI&DS) at AISSMS Institute of Information Technology (IOIT), Pune, successfully organised the two-day AI Summit 2026 on October 27 and 28. Chhatrapati Maloji Raje, Secretary, AISSMS Society; Dr. Pradeep B. Mane, Principal, AISSMS IOIT; and Dr. R. A. Jamadar, Head of the Department of AI&DS.The event was coordinated by the Artificial Intelligence Student Association (AISA) under the guidance of Dr. P. B. Wakhare, Programme Coordinator. The individual event coordinators were Dr. Pradnya D. Bormane for the keynote sessions, Dr. Shagupta Shaikh for the panel discussion, and Dr. D. S. articles.summary: Public school closures are accelerating across the country, and voters in several states have a chance to speed up or slow down the process Tuesday. articles.body:
Public school closures are accelerating across the country, and voters in several states have a chance to speed up or slow down the process Tuesday.

Closures are largely determined by school board members and affected by a district’s funding situation, which itself is downstream from state legislatures and governors’ mansions.

With school board seats up for grabs and more than 12 states with ballot initiatives affecting school funding, these midterms could bring some relief to parents who are dissatisfied with plans to shut down more school buildings.

“This is one of the least popular things a district can do, and so it would be very difficult for a candidate to run on a pro-closure platform. On the other hand, you do have some candidates who have said, ‘We have steep, declining enrollment. We need to align the number of schools we have with the number of students we have. We need to shrink to match our circumstances,'” said Carrie Hahnel, a partner at Bellwether, an education research nonprofit.

“It’ll be interesting to see if there are communities that are sympathetic to that,” Hahnel added.

The enrollment crisis is a problem across the country, affecting major cities including Chicago, Los Angeles and Seattle.

Researchers found public schools lost 1.83 million students between the 2019-2020 school year and the 2023-2024 one, a shift fueled by the pandemic.

The National Center for Education Statistics projects public school enrollment will drop 7.5 percent from 2019 to 2031.

And there is not much districts can do about it, as most of the decline is from falling birth rates in the U.S., although some of it is also coming from shifts in education and greater participation in school choice programs.

Since enrollment is directly linked to funding, schools start to feel the pinch in their pockets pretty quickly.

Minneapolis Public Schools (MPS), a district that serves more than 29,000 students, tabled plans to talk about school closures until next year, after years of funding declines took away popular programs and fears of immigration enforcement have impacted enrollment.

That puts the issue squarely on the nine candidates who are running to join the school board.

“I think that’s something that gets lost sometimes in these closure discussions. There are enough students in the district to get up to operational efficiency, if that’s what you want to call it. This is not the same situation as you see out in rural areas, where schools have to close because of demographic shifts. MPS has opportunity,” school board candidate Ben Lattimore said in an interview with the Sahan Journal.

Some states do have programs that allow schools to retain a certain level of funding despite enrollment drops to give a brief reprieve for a few years, but they are not popular with lawmakers or sustainable in the long term.

“Some legislatures might come in and say, ‘We’ll do a one-year hold harmless or a two-year hold harmless that gives districts some time, potentially, or some reprieve in the short term.’ Those policies are expensive for legislatures,” said Marguerite Roza, director of the Edunomics Lab at Georgetown University.

While school boards ultimately vote on the issue, state guidance and politics affect their decisions.

“What will have a major impact on [school closures] are the changing politics and policies that could be the result of the midterm elections. And so, with 36 states electing governors this year, that has major implications for the school board makeup, for the makeup of chief school officers and what they have the power to do to help districts navigate this difficulty,” said Nithya Joseph, managing partner of policy and advocacy at TNTP, a nonprofit that works with schools to redesign education systems.

Gubernatorial races in numerous states have seen staunch stances on school choice, with Democratic opponents attacking their counterparts for sending money out of public schools at a time when the institutions are struggling.

Ohio Democratic governor hopeful Amy Acton’s campaign website says “public money should be for public schools” and that she wants to “reform” the “corrupt school voucher system” in the state.

Vivek Ramaswamy, her Republican opponent, has eagerly supported Ohio’s school choice program and says public schools need to improve outcomes for more funding.

“Well, I want to talk about outcomes, and then what we need to get those outcomes, we’ll talk about for funding,” Ramaswamy said, as reported by the Ohio Capital Journal . “But it’s a school debate, school policy debate — should not be an accounting debate.”

Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor in Texas, has run on a “save Texas public schools” platform against Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term.

“Gina rejects spending big money on school vouchers and expensive vendors. As Governor, Gina will end the voucher scam and ensure Texans’ taxpayer dollars go where they belong: into the neighborhood schools families depend on,” Hinojosa’s campaign website reads.

The state politics around funding and support for public schools could be an influential factor when districts decide whether to close buildings.

“Because while it’s a set of undesirable challenges that districts are facing, and that school closures and consolidations may be a reality in those sets of decisions, how those decisions are made are really impacted by the guidance that these state-level education leaders can really provide these districts as they’re navigating this tough time,” Joseph said.

In 2022, the Oakland Unified School District board in California approved a plan to close schools because of funding difficulties. That plan was reversed in 2023, when three new members were added to the school board.

But experts warn these victories are often short-lived.

“I would say to communities, ‘Be careful what you wish for,’ because it’s not like the financial pain goes away if you change the board member, and it’s the financial pain and the enrollment declines that are causing that response from the board that we may need to close schools,” Roza said.

School closures are a top issue again in the Oakland school board race, as the district still has a $38 million deficit.

There are ways some schools have avoided closures despite declining enrollment and funding, but it typically involves cutting programs or classes and making some positions, such as counselors, part time.

While school closures are more of a state and local issue, the federal government could make the situation harder by cutting back funding to states.

“If we have a Congress that continues to want to cut overall funding, well, some of those programs are still going to run even if the funding isn’t there,” said Noelle Ellerson Ng, chief advocacy and governance officer at the School Superintendents Association.

“So, then you’ll start to see state and local education agencies use their own dollars to cover that shortfall, and that’s where you might start to see more impact on funding that is available for keeping schools open or the like, because that money will come from the budget, and if it has to be reallocated to cover a shortfall elsewhere, they’re not going to be able to do it that way,” she added.

articles.title: Isabel, de 77 años, y Mario, de 81, dan su segunda vuelta al mundo tras jubilarse: "Sin prisa, pero sin pausa"
articles.standfirst: Isabel Rodríguez y Mario Ubach aprovechan su jubilación para viajar por los cinco continentes
articles.summary: Isabel Rodríguez y Mario Ubach aprovechan su jubilación para viajar por los cinco continentes
articles.body: La jubilación suele asociarse al descanso después de décadas de trabajo, pero Isabel Rodríguez y Mario Ubach han decidido aprovechar esta etapa para cumplir uno de los sueños que tuvieron que aplazar durante años: recorrer el mundo. Ella tiene 77 años y él, 81, y llevan una década compartiendo sus aventuras viajeras, una experiencia que les ha permitido conocer los cinco continentes y acumular recorridos que ellos mismos calculan que equivalen a dos vueltas al mundo. La pareja, procedente de Barcelona, tiene un pasado profesional ligado al ámbito sanitario. Isabel trabajó como enfermera y Mario como cirujano. Durante 24 años también estuvieron vinculados a proyectos de cooperación sanitaria, una etapa que les permitió conocer distintos países, aunque las obligaciones laborales y familiares impedían realizar los grandes viajes que tenían en mente. La idea de aprovechar la jubilación para viajar llevaba tiempo entre sus planes. En 2015 abrieron el blog 'Con más de 70', donde comenzaron a compartir sus experiencias y consejos con otros viajeros. En su propia presentación explican que siempre les había fascinado conocer qué había más allá de su entorno cotidiano y que esperaron a disponer del tiempo necesario para emprender esa aventura. Su forma de viajar también rompe con algunos de los tópicos asociados a las vacaciones de las personas mayores. Isabel y Mario se desplazan como mochileros y prefieren organizar sus recorridos con bastante libertad. Según explicó la pareja, suelen reservar los vuelos y las primeras noches de alojamiento, mientras que el resto del itinerario lo van improvisando sobre la marcha. En sus viajes optan por hoteles modestos, mercados locales y transportes compartidos. Su primer gran recorrido después de la jubilación fue de cuatro meses por el sudeste asiático. Posteriormente pasaron seis meses entre Filipinas, Japón y Nueva Zelanda, antes de continuar sus aventuras por América Latina, con visitas a países como Chile, Bolivia, México, Guatemala, Panamá, Colombia y República Dominicana. Entre los lugares que más les han marcado mencionan Australia, el Congo, Japón y Madagascar. En febrero de 2026, Isabel y Mario se encontraban en Colombia, donde habían disfrutado del Carnaval de Barranquilla. También habían pasado por Praga, donde Isabel participó en una actividad con un coro. La edad tampoco ha impedido que sigan viajando, aunque sí han tenido que adaptar algunos planes. Mario lleva prótesis de rodilla y cadera y necesita revisiones médicas periódicas. Además, se han encontrado con restricciones de edad para determinadas actividades. En Colombia, por ejemplo, no pudieron realizar una ruta de senderismo al Nevado del Ruiz debido al límite recomendado para participar en ella. Isabel también ha desarrollado una faceta literaria durante esta etapa. Ha escrito la novela solidaria 'Maruja', cuyos beneficios se destinan a una fundación. Su filosofía queda resumida en una expresión que repiten al hablar de sus viajes: "Sin prisa, pero sin pausa". Una forma de entender la jubilación que les ha llevado a convertir el tiempo libre en una oportunidad para seguir descubriendo lugares, culturas y experiencias.

articles.title: Charter school founder backs Trump administration push to decentralize K-12 education
articles.summary: Salt Lake City charter school founder Carolyn Sharette backs the Trump administration's efforts to cut federal red tape and return education to states.
articles.body: SALT LAKE CITY — A charter school founder and executive is throwing her support behind the Trump administration’s effort to strip federal bureaucracy from classrooms and return education authority to the states. "It is very helpful to return the funding to the states that we already get, but with less regulation on those funds so that I can serve our students' needs — precisely what they need — instead of maybe what somebody in Washington thought they needed," Carolyn Sharette, founder and executive director of American Preparatory Academy (APA), told Fox News Digital. Sharette founded APA in Utah in 2003. The public charter school network now serves more than 5,000 students across eight Utah campuses. DENVER MOTHER FIGHTS FOR HER DAUGHTER'S EDUCATION AS ADVOCATES MAKE NATIONWIDE SCHOOL CHOICE PUSH "We know exactly what our students need here to progress, and so returning the education to the states means we get to use the money in more flexible ways to help our students," Sharette said. On Oct. 20, APA’s West Valley City campus served as the 47th stop on Education Secretary Linda McMahon’s 50-state "Returning Education to the States Tour," which aims to highlight the Trump administration's K-12 reform efforts. Delivering a keynote speech titled "The Next 250: K-12 Education," McMahon emphasized shifting authority back to local leaders, investing in proven academic interventions and expanding school choice for families. According to U.S. Department of Education officials, more than $3 trillion in federal taxpayer money has been funneled into K-12 education in recent decades. Despite the massive expenditure, national assessment data shows only about three in 10 students perform at or above proficient levels in math and reading. AMERICAN SCHOOLS COST MORE THAN EVER BUT OUR STUDENTS STILL KEEP FAILING Upon taking office, McMahon pledged to work toward dismantling the federal education agency, including installing leaders tasked with phasing out their own divisions. The effort aligns with President Donald Trump’s broader educational agenda, which he highlighted during a White House Rose Garden event championing school choice. "School choice is really profound, actually," Sharette told Fox News Digital. "The role we play because we provide a place for parents to choose a different school if they'd like, and it's wonderful that they have that option." MCMAHON PLANS TO 'FIRE' HERSELF FROM A JOB, STRIVING TO SHOW CONGRESS THAT THE DEPARTMENT OF ED IS NOT NEEDED "We provide a school that is a classical school," Sharette added. "We teach through literature, we teach the science of reading. We've always had very high reading scores at our school. So parents who are looking for a rigorous and classical education can choose our school and have that freedom." Trump has also pledged to eliminate "far-left extremism" from classrooms, arguing that decades of federal administrative oversight have failed to yield acceptable academic results. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP To streamline operations, the Department of Education recently launched a new waiver process allowing state leaders to request greater flexibility when spending federal funds, while significantly cutting administrative red tape. Iowa became the first state in the nation to participate in the flexibility initiative.

articles.title: Exit exams out, mediocrity in: The decline and fall of US graduation standards
articles.summary: We can measure whether students can multiply and whether certain instructional practices helped them do it. But how do we measure global citizenship? We can’t, and so anything goes.
articles.body:
Last month, the New York State Education Department announced that it intends to nix the Regents Exam as a graduation requirement in the Empire State.

The policy change received widespread condemnation. Former Gov. George Pataki (R) ripped the move as “incredibly stupid.” The Wall Street Journal editorial board criticized it as “as one more sorry milestone on America’s educational march to mediocrity.”

They’re right to heap scorn on the change. It’s entirely appropriate to test and ensure that graduates leave high school with basic competencies in reading, writing, and math. Receiving less opprobrium, but equally deserving of it, is what will replace the exam itself .

Education Commissioner Betty Rosa has explained that instead of relying on the Regents, the state is building a “graduation system grounded in New York’s Portrait of a Graduate,” a program wherein students can demonstrate their learning through performance-based assessments and portfolios. Instead of simply passing a basic competency test, the Portrait of a Graduate requires that students demonstrate their ability to be a “critical thinker” and “global citizen” through “multiple measures.”

Such banalities are superficially appealing — after all, who would oppose critical thinking? But the ability to think critically relies upon rudimentary academic skills of the kind the Regents Exam tested. No student can meaningfully analyze current events without basic factual knowledge of history or the ability to read paragraphs and comprehend them.

These portraits replace with vague aspirations the concrete, measurable, academic benchmarks that allow for higher-level cognitive functions. Consequently, students are likely to develop neither.

New York is actually late to this trend. In the mid-2000s, 27 states required high school exit exams. That number is now down to just six. Concurrently, 26 states have adopted some variation of “ Portrait of a Graduate ,” so we have evidence of what these shifts mean in practice.

A 2024 report by the ed-tech nonprofit Digital Promise analyzed more than 60 graduate portraits from districts. It devised a model for districts to follow that it says incorporates 90 percent of the specific competencies that appear across their sample. These include an ability to “care for and contribute to society” and “communicate in all media and modalities.”

In their report, they include models of what such a Portrait might look like in practice. For example, Digital Promise recommends middle school students demonstrate their problem-solving abilities through spaghetti tower challenges .

Another performance task that the ed-tech lauds comes by way of Howard-Suamico, Wisconsin , where students demonstrate “collaboration” by crafting tri-fold posters about potential gluten-free Taco trucks. Even the student model includes basic errors — get your taco with “ sweat corn .”

I was once a teacher. I don’t fault students for letting a typo slip through here or there. I have seen plenty of last-minute projects cobbled together the night before. But when such work is set forth as the ideal, it makes the whole effort look like a method to justify seemingly everything except academics.

Battelle for Kids, one of the main organizations behind the trend toward measurements such as “Portraits of a Graduate,” sets forth as an exemplar a student presentation analyzing Tupac and Lil Wayne lyrics from Affton School District in Missouri. It holds up as another example a collage of political posters on gun control and abortion rights in Winston-Salem, N.C.

In other words, by adopting poorly defined and unmeasurable goals, schools can use almost any activity to demonstrate preferred competencies. Running in parallel, schools can then also explain away academic failure. Sure, the students may not be able to add fractions, and they can’t name the three branches of government, but fortunately we have abolished all the tools we once had to measure such failures.

We can measure whether students can multiply and whether certain instructional practices helped them do it. But how do we measure global citizenship and determine if any one activity or another fosters it? We can’t, and so anything goes. Oh well — at least they can all conspicuously “ embrace diversity !”

Most everyone hopes that schools will foster some competencies, such as perseverance or problem-solving. But they are situated to do so best when they emphasize traditional academics.

How can a school foster grit? Maintain demanding academic gauntlets. How can schools create self-discipline? Set behavioral standards and hold students to them. How can schools enable critical thinking? Provide them the knowledge of history, science, literature, grammar, and the arts that become the tools of critical thought.

Students become thoughtful, self-controlled citizens by wrestling with worthy subject matter, not through kitschy activities where they make posters about how kindness is cool.

Getting rid of the Regents Exams was a mistake, but what they are replacing it with might be even worse.

Daniel Buck is a research fellow and the director of the Conservative Education Reform Network at the American Enterprise Institute.

articles.title: La advertencia viral de una abogada sobre el voto en el 29N: "Si no eres millonario, párate a pensar qué vas a votar"
articles.standfirst: Sandra Burgos, abogada de familia, rompe la neutralidad política pese al acoso en redes
articles.summary: Sandra Burgos, abogada de familia, rompe la neutralidad política pese al acoso en redes
articles.body: La abogada de familia Sandra Burgos ha decidido romper públicamente su habitual neutralidad política pese a saber que iba a sufrir una oleada de ataques en las redes sociales que califica de "siderales". Pese a perder más de medio millar de seguidores en un solo día, afirma con rotundidad: "He perdido más de 500 seguidores en las últimas 24 horas y os digo una cosa, me da igual". Burgos explica que, aunque históricamente se ha mantenido al margen de la política partidista, el contexto actual le impide continuar al margen. En sus propias palabras, argumenta que "la postura neutral lo que lleva es a muchas veces a que al final te acaben restringiendo tus propios derechos". Alejada de etiquetas ideológicas extremas, se define como una ciudadana conservadora cuyo único anhelo es poder ir a trabajar, pagar sus impuestos y vivir con tranquilidad. La abogada alerta de que las propuestas de la derecha y la ultraderecha ponen en riesgo pilares fundamentales del bienestar social. En este sentido, lanza una advertencia directa a la ciudadanía sobre los programas electorales y la sanidad pública: "Si no sois millonarios y Dios no lo quiera, contraéis un cáncer, pensad que como mínimo tendréis que tener unos 300.000 euros para poder combatir ese cáncer". Del mismo modo, cuestiona cómo las familias trabajadoras afrontarán la privatización de la educación o la pérdida de derechos reproductivos adquiridos con esfuerzo durante generaciones. Asimismo, trata el derecho a una muerte digna, recordando que cuenta con su testamento vital en regla para evitar sufrimientos innecesarios. Defiende que "la eutanasia es un derecho, no es una obligación" y denuncia que no quiere que le arrebaten conquistas sociales esenciales como la sanidad pública, el derecho al voto o la propia dignidad al final de la vida. Un debate actual que para ella no responde a una simple división entre derechas e izquierdas, sino a una cuestión básica de pura lógica. Sandra Burgos concluye su reflexión con un llamamiento urgente a la reflexión de cara a las próximas citas con las urnas. Dirigiéndose tanto a mujeres como a hombres que no forman parte de las élites económicas, insiste en la necesidad de analizar minuciosamente los programas políticos. Su mensaje concluye con una premisa clara y directa para el electorado: "Si no eres millonario, párate lo que vas a votar", recordando que la pérdida de derechos públicos afecta directamente a la supervivencia y dignidad de las próximas generaciones.
